chapters.title: Computer Organization — Instruction Cycle and Microprogrammed Control

questions.title: Fetch Sequence
questions.question: The sequence of events that happens during a typical fetch operation is:
questions.solution: The PC supplies the instruction address to MAR; memory returns the instruction to MDR, and it is then loaded into IR.

questions.title: Load Accumulator Micro-operations
questions.question: Which set of micro-operations transfers the memory word specified by the effective address to AC (Load to AC)?
options: DR ← [MAR], AC ← AC + DR, E ← Cout, SC ← 0
questions.solution: A load operation reads the memory word into a data register and then transfers it to AC. The other options describe store or arithmetic behavior, or add an unrelated carry update.

questions.title: Horizontal Microprogram Control Word
questions.question: A CPU has 128 instructions, each operation needs 8 cycles, and 60 control signals must be generated. If a single signal-address field format is used, what is the minimum control-word size for horizontal microprogramming?
questions.solution: A signal-address field needs ceil(log₂60) = 6 bits to identify one of 60 control signals. With 60 control-signal bits in horizontal form, the wording/options may be using a different encoding assumption; 67 is the likely intended option (60 + 7 address/sequence bits). The question's exact control-word format is underspecified.

questions.title: Address Bits for Branch Control
questions.question: A single address-field format is used for branch control logic. The control word is 64 bits wide. The control portion is divided into a 24-bit micro-operation field and an address-selection field specifying a condition based on 16 flags. How many bits remain for the address field?
questions.solution: The remaining bits are 64 − 24 − log₂(16) = 64 − 24 − 4 = 36 if the 4-bit condition selector is part of the word. If 'address bits' means the branch target field, the answer is 36. The question wording calls the address-selection field a condition field, so this interpretation should be checked against the source's intended format.

questions.title: CISC Architecture
questions.question: Which statement is false about CISC architecture?
options: CISC machine instructions may include complex addressing modes that require many clock cycles.
CISC control units are typically microprogrammed, allowing the instruction set to be more flexible.
In the CISC instruction set, all arithmetic/logic instructions must be register-based.
questions.solution: CISC instructions may support memory operands and complex addressing modes; arithmetic/logic instructions are not required to be exclusively register-based.

questions.title: Indirect Operand Fetch Microprogram
questions.question: Which option shows the microprogram for an indirect operand fetch cycle?
options: t₁: MAR ← IR[Address], t₂: MBR ← Memory[MAR], t₃: AC ← MBR
t₁: MAR ← (PC), t₂: MBR ← Memory, PC ← (PC) + 1, t₃: IR ← MBR
t₁: MAR ← (IR[Address]), t₂: MBR ← Memory, t₃: MAR ← MBR, t₄: MBR ← Memory, t₅: Accumulator ← MBR
questions.solution: Indirect addressing first reads the address stored at the instruction's address field, then uses that fetched address to read the operand. The exact notation depends on the source's register conventions.

questions.title: Indirect Addressing Memory Cycles
questions.question: For operand fetch using indirect addressing, how many memory cycles are required to bring the operand into the CPU?
questions.solution: Typically, one memory access obtains the effective address from the indirect address field and a second obtains the operand. This excludes the earlier instruction-fetch cycle.

questions.title: Horizontal versus Vertical Control Bits
questions.question: A microprogrammed control unit supports 7 groups of mutually exclusive control signals: Gr1 (2), Gr2 (10), Gr3 (4), Gr4 (1), Gr5 (18), Gr6 (23), Gr7 (6). How many more control bits does horizontal microprogramming require than vertical microprogramming?
questions.solution: Horizontal bits = 2+10+4+1+18+23+6 = 64. Vertical encoding needs Σceil(log₂(group size + 1)) = 2+4+3+1+5+5+3 = 23 bits, including a no-signal code in each group. Difference = 41 bits. If the convention uses ceil(log₂ n) without a no-signal code, the result differs; confirm the course convention.

questions.title: Horizontal and Vertical Control Signals
questions.question: A hypothetical control unit has 512 bytes of control-word memory. The control word is 20 bits long, the hardware has 4 flags, and it supports 16 branch conditions. What is the maximum number of control signals generated at a time using horizontal and vertical microprogramming, respectively?
questions.solution: Horizontal microprogramming uses individual control bits, allowing many signals to be asserted simultaneously; vertical microprogramming encodes control choices, typically selecting one operation per encoded field. The intended answer is 32, 1, although the stated 20-bit word makes the 32 figure inconsistent without further assumptions.

questions.title: Control Unit Speed
questions.question: Among vertical microprogramming, horizontal microprogramming, and hardwired control, which has the highest and lowest operational speed, respectively?
questions.solution: Hardwired control is generally fastest. Vertical microprogramming is generally slower than horizontal microprogramming because it requires decoding. The original asks for highest and lowest, so both statements (a) and (c) are correct; this is effectively a multiple-select question despite the MCQ label.

chapters.title: Computer Organization — Memory Addressing and Cache

questions.title: Word-Addressable Memory Address Bus
questions.question: A processor supports a maximum memory of 8 GB, and memory is word-addressable with 1 word = 2 bytes. What is the minimum address-bus size?
questions.solution: 8 GB = 2³³ bytes. With 2 bytes per addressable word, there are 2³² addressable words, requiring 32 address bits. The provided options make 32 bits the correct result; answer index 1.

questions.title: Direct-Mapped Cache Tag Bits
questions.question: A direct-mapped cache has 8 lines, each line holds 2 words, each word is 1 byte, and the address bus is 7 bits. How many bits are in the tag field?
questions.solution: Block offset = log₂(2 bytes) = 1 bit. Index = log₂(8 lines) = 3 bits. Tag = 7 − 1 − 3 = 3 bits.

questions.title: Four-Way Cache Tag Bits
questions.question: A 32-bit address system has a cache of 2 MB with block size 8 KB. How many tag bits are required for a 4-way set-associative cache?
questions.solution: Block offset = log₂(8 KB) = 13 bits. Number of sets = 2 MB / (8 KB × 4) = 64, so index = 6 bits. Tag = 32 − 13 − 6 = 13 bits. The stated cache size/block size gives 13, not 11.

questions.title: Cache Blocks and Tag Size
questions.question: A 16-KB cache has 32-byte blocks, is 2-way set associative, uses 32-bit physical byte addresses, and each word is 32 bits. How many blocks are in the cache, and how many tag bits are stored per block?
questions.solution: Number of blocks = 16 KB / 32 B = 512. Sets = 512 / 2 = 256, index = 8 bits, block offset = 5 bits, so tag = 32 − 8 − 5 = 19 bits.

questions.title: Index Bits in Set-Associative and Fully Associative Cache
questions.question: A 16-KB, 2-way set-associative cache has 32-byte lines and a 64-bit address space. Let p be the index bits. If the cache were fully associative, let q be the index bits. What is p + q?
questions.solution: There are 16 KB / 32 B = 512 lines. For 2-way associativity, sets = 256, so p = 8. A fully associative cache has one set, so q = 0. Therefore p + q = 8.

questions.title: Number of L2 Cache Lines
questions.question: A 512-KB, 16-way set-associative L2 cache has a 128-byte cache line. How many cache lines are present?
questions.solution: Number of lines = cache size / line size = 512 × 1024 / 128 = 4096.

questions.title: Cache Associativity from Tag Size
questions.question: A cache uses 32-bit addresses, has 768 blocks, block size 128 bytes, and 17-bit tags. What is the associativity?
questions.solution: Offset = 7 bits; index = 32 − 17 − 7 = 8 bits, implying 256 sets. Associativity = 768 / 256 = 3 ways, so the answer is 3-way. The given quantities are unusual but mathematically imply 3-way associativity.

questions.title: Direct-Mapped Cache Contents
questions.question: A direct-mapped cache has 16 blocks (0–15), and main memory has blocks 0–255. Initially the cache is empty. Memory-block references are 3, 180, 43, 2, 191, 881, 190, 14, 181, 44, 186, 253. Which blocks are in the cache after the sequence?
questions.solution: The reference 881 is outside the stated main-memory block range 0–255, and the answer choices do not cleanly represent the final direct-mapped cache state. The question appears to contain transcription errors; none of the listed states can be reliably validated as written.

questions.title: Probability of Cache Hit
questions.question: For the access pattern x, y, z, y, x, each letter is a unique cache block. No blocks were accessed before this. What is the probability that the second access to x is a hit on a direct-mapped cache with 4 lines, assuming conflicts are random?
questions.solution: With distinct blocks x, y, and z mapping to distinct cache lines under the stated simple interpretation, x remains in the cache until its second access, so the hit probability is 100%. The phrase 'conflicts are random' is ambiguous and may indicate omitted assumptions.

questions.title: Fastest Cache Mapping
questions.question: Which is the fastest cache mapping function among the following?
questions.solution: Direct mapping is generally the simplest and fastest because the index selects exactly one cache line, avoiding associative tag searches.

questions.title: Effective Memory Access Time
questions.question: A cache has a 70% hit ratio, access time of 50 ns on a hit, and access time of 120 ns on a miss. What is the effective access time?
questions.solution: Using the stated hit and miss access times as complete alternatives: EAT = 0.7×50 + 0.3×120 = 35 + 36 = 71 ns, which is not listed. If 120 ns is a miss penalty added after cache access, EAT = 50 + 0.3×120 = 86 ns. The likely intended convention gives 86 ns.

questions.title: Average Access Time for Two-Level Cache
questions.question: The local hit rate for L1 is 20% and for L2 is 30%. L1 hit time is 8 cycles, L2 hit time is 20 cycles, and main-memory access time is 30 cycles. What is the approximate average memory access time?
questions.solution: Using local hit rates: AMAT = 8 + (1−0.20)×[20 + (1−0.30)×30] = 8 + 0.8×41 = 40.8 cycles, approximately 41.

questions.title: Cache Memory Properties
questions.question: Choose the correct statements about cache memory.
options: Instructions and data stored in cache are regularly used by the CPU; if data is not present in cache, it always transfers from main memory.
Data is stored on a temporary basis in cache memory.
Programs stored in cache take more time to execute.
questions.solution: Cache is a small, fast memory that temporarily stores copies of data/instructions. It has limited capacity. A miss may be served by another cache level or memory, and cache does not make programs slower in general.

questions.title: Compulsory and Conflict Misses
questions.question: Consider the statements: S1: Increasing block size can reduce compulsory misses. S2: Increasing cache associativity can increase conflict misses.
options: Both S1 and S2 are true
Neither S1 nor S2 is true
questions.solution: Larger blocks can exploit spatial locality and reduce compulsory misses. Increasing associativity generally reduces conflict misses, rather than increasing them.

questions.title: Average Cache Access Time with Write-Back
questions.question: A 128-word cache has 32-word blocks. Main-memory access time is 50 µs/word and cache access time is 20 µs/word. Read hit ratio is 80%, write hit ratio is 90%, and 40% of references are writes. On a miss, the block is brought from main memory for both reads and writes. With write-back, 80% of cache blocks are modified at any point, calculate average access time (µs, to 1 decimal).
questions.solution: The question does not specify whether the 50 µs/word memory time applies to every word transferred in a block, nor the write-back dirty-block write time and exact miss accounting. A unique numeric answer cannot be determined without those conventions.

questions.title: Addressable Memory Size from Cache Parameters
questions.question: A 16-way set-associative cache of size 128 KB is used in a system with 32-bit addresses. Block size is 4 bytes. What is the memory size in KB?
questions.solution: The address width identifies an address space, not necessarily a physical memory size in KB without knowing whether addresses are byte-addressed and whether all 32-bit addresses are implemented. Under byte addressing, 32 bits can address 2³² bytes = 4 GiB; the cache parameters do not change that address-space limit.

questions.title: IEEE 754 Single Precision to Decimal
questions.question: Convert the IEEE single-precision bit pattern `01000011110100000000000000000000` to decimal.
questions.solution: Sign = 0. Exponent bits 10000111₂ = 135, so unbiased exponent = 135−127 = 8. Fraction is 1.101₂ = 1.625. Value = 1.625×2⁸ = 416.

questions.title: Hexadecimal IEEE 754 Value
questions.question: What decimal value is represented by IEEE 754 single-precision hexadecimal `0x43758000`?
questions.solution: Decoding 0x43758000 as IEEE 754 single precision gives 245.5. This is not among the listed values, so choose None of the above.

questions.title: IEEE 754 Special Value
questions.question: In IEEE 754 single precision, what does `11111111100000000000000000000000` represent?
questions.solution: The sign bit is 1, exponent is all ones, and fraction is all zeros, which represents negative infinity.

questions.title: Hexadecimal Negative Float
questions.question: What decimal value is represented by IEEE 754 single-precision hexadecimal `0xC4127000`?
questions.solution: Decoding 0xC4127000 as IEEE 754 single precision gives -585.75. This is not among the listed values, so choose None of these.

questions.title: IEEE 754 Representation of 16
questions.question: Which is the IEEE 754 32-bit floating-point representation of 16?
questions.solution: 16 = 1.0×2⁴. Sign = 0, exponent = 127+4 = 131 = 10000011₂, fraction = all zeros. Thus the representation is 0 10000011 000…000.

questions.title: Binary IEEE 754 Value
questions.question: What decimal value is represented by the IEEE 754 single-precision bit pattern `0 10000111 11110100000000000000000`?
questions.solution: Exponent = 135−127 = 8. Significand = 1.111101₂ = 1.953125. Value = 1.953125×256 = 500, so option (c) is correct. The exact bit pattern should be checked: 111101 fraction corresponds to 1.953125.

chapters.title: Computer Organization — Registers, Memory Organization and Endianness

questions.title: Word Addressing and Saved Address Pins
questions.question: A 64-bit hypothetical CPU supports a 256-KB memory space and uses word-addressable memory. How many address pins are saved compared with byte addressing if a word is 8 bytes?
questions.solution: A word of 8 bytes means each address identifies 8 bytes, reducing address bits by log₂(8) = 3 compared with byte addressing.

questions.title: RAM Chip Count
questions.question: How many 128 × 8-bit RAM chips are required to design a 32K × 32-bit RAM?
questions.solution: Depth expansion: 32K/128 = 256. Width expansion: 32/8 = 4. Total chips = 256×4 = 1024, so option (b) is correct.

questions.title: Program Counter During Instruction Execution
questions.question: A 32-bit hypothetical CPU uses word-addressable memory. Code starts at address 2000. Instruction sizes are I1=16 bytes, I2=12 bytes, I3=16 bytes, I4=12 bytes, I5=8 bytes, I6=8 bytes. During execution of I4, what is the PC value?
questions.solution: With 4-byte words, instruction sizes are 4, 3, 4, 3, 2, 2 words. I4 starts after I1–I3: 2000 + 4 + 3 + 4 = 2011. If PC points to the current instruction, 2011 is the address; the source's phrasing may instead refer to the next instruction.

questions.title: CPU Register Matching
questions.question: Match Column I with Column II: A. PC; B. MAR; C. IR; D. AC. (i) instruction currently being executed; (ii) temporary result/first ALU operand; (iii) starting address of next instruction to fetch; (iv) address of memory location used for read/write.
questions.solution: PC stores the next instruction address; MAR stores the memory address for a read/write; IR stores the current instruction; AC stores an operand or intermediate ALU result.

questions.title: 8085 Load Add Store Program
questions.question: What does this 8085 program do? `LDA 8000H; MVI B, 30H; ADD B; STA 8001H`
options: Read a number from an input port and store it in memory.
Read a number from input device address 8000H and store it in memory.
Read a number from memory location 8000H, add 30H, and store the result at memory location 8001H.
questions.solution: LDA loads the accumulator from memory address 8000H; MVI loads 30H into B; ADD B adds B to A; STA stores A at 8001H.

questions.title: PC with Byte-Addressable Memory
questions.question: A 64-bit hypothetical CPU uses byte-addressable memory. Code starts at address 1000. Instruction sizes are I1=2 bytes, I2=4 bytes, I3=4 bytes, I4=4 bytes, I5=2 bytes, I6=6 bytes. During execution of I5, what is the PC value?
questions.solution: I5 begins after I1–I4: 1000+2+4+4+4 = 1014. If PC points to the current instruction, it is 1014; if it points to the next instruction during execution, it is 1016. The intended convention must be clarified.

questions.title: Instruction Transfer over an 8-bit Bus
questions.question: An instruction is 32 bits and the bus has 8 lines, transferring 1 byte per memory access. How many memory accesses are required to transfer the instruction?
questions.solution: 32 bits = 4 bytes. At 1 byte per access, 4 memory accesses are required.

questions.title: Endianness
questions.question: Consider: S1: In little endian, the lower address contains the lower byte and the higher address contains the higher byte. S2: In big endian, the lower address contains the higher byte and the higher address contains the lower byte.
options: Both S1 and S2 are true
Neither S1 nor S2 is true
questions.solution: Little endian stores the least-significant byte at the lowest address; big endian stores the most-significant byte at the lowest address.

questions.title: Accumulator and Program Counter
questions.question: Consider: S1: The accumulator stores results of calculations made by the ALU. S2: The program counter keeps track of the memory location of the current instruction being processed.
options: Both S1 and S2 are true
Neither S1 nor S2 is true
questions.solution: S1 is generally true. The PC typically contains the address of the next instruction to fetch, not necessarily the current instruction's address.

questions.title: Register Functions
questions.question: Which statements are true?
options: MAR stores the memory address needed for a memory access.
MDR stores an instruction fetched from memory or data being transferred to/from memory.
IR stores the most recently fetched instruction.
The instruction buffer register contains instructions not to be executed immediately.
questions.solution: These are the standard functions of MAR, MDR/MBR, IR, and an instruction buffer register, respectively, subject to architecture-specific naming.

chapters.title: Computer Organization — Instruction Formats and Addressing Modes

questions.title: Primitive Instruction Format
questions.question: Which of the following is a primitive instruction format in the CPU?
options: opcode (4 bits), Address-1 (4 bits), Address-2 (4 bits)
opcode (2 bits), Address-1 (12 bits), Address-2 (8 bits)
questions.solution: The question does not define 'primitive instruction'. Option (a) is a conventional one-address format, but the intended answer cannot be established from the provided wording alone.

questions.title: Opcode Count for Two-Address Instructions
questions.question: A hypothetical system supports only two-address instructions. Instruction size is 28 bits and each address is 10 bits. What is the maximum number of instructions supported?
questions.solution: Opcode bits = 28 − 2×10 = 8. Maximum distinct opcodes = 2⁸ = 256.

questions.title: Three-Address Instruction Size
questions.question: A digital computer supports 64 three-address instructions. Each address is 14 bits. What is the instruction size in bytes, assuming a fixed-length format?
questions.solution: 64 instructions need 6 opcode bits. Total instruction size = 6 + 3×14 = 48 bits = 6 bytes. The correct numeric answer is 6, not 7.

questions.title: Fetch-Execute Cycle Order
questions.question: What is the correct sequence in the fetch-execute cycle?
questions.solution: The instruction is fetched from memory, decoded by the control unit, and then executed.

questions.title: Instruction Size with Two Addresses
questions.question: A system supports only two-address instructions and has 2^p KB of memory. If it supports q distinct instructions, what is the instruction size?
questions.solution: If memory is byte-addressable, 2^p KB = 2^(p+10) bytes, so each address needs p+10 bits. The opcode needs ceil(log₂q) bits. Total = log₂q + 2(p+10) bits, assuming q is a power of two.

questions.title: Mixed One- and Two-Address Opcodes
questions.question: A system supports both two-address and one-address instructions. Instruction length is 6 bits and each address is 2 bits. If there are three two-address instructions, what is the maximum and minimum number of one-address instructions?
questions.solution: A 6-bit instruction with two 2-bit addresses leaves 2 opcode bits for two-address forms. The prefix/opcode allocation needed to determine the remaining one-address encodings is not specified sufficiently by the question; none of the options can be validated unambiguously.

questions.title: PC-Relative Branch Address
questions.question: A PC-relative branch targets address 680 and has offset 420. What is the instruction address if each instruction occupies two memory locations?
questions.solution: PC-relative target calculations depend on whether the PC is the instruction address or the next-instruction address, and on whether the offset is measured in bytes or instruction words. The question does not specify these conventions clearly enough to choose reliably.

questions.title: Instruction Fetch and Execution Time
questions.question: A 6-word instruction has fields opcode, Mode-1, Mode-2, Address-1, Address-2. The destination uses register-indirect mode and the source uses indirect mode. Each operand and each address occupy 2 words; memory takes 20 ns per word access. Register access time is negligible. What is the difference between instruction fetch time and execution time?
questions.solution: The stated instruction length and field sizes are inconsistent unless the field layout is clarified. Execution-time counting also depends on whether the indirect pointer and operand reads each require two word accesses. Cannot determine a unique answer as written.

questions.title: Zero-Address Instruction Count
questions.question: A computer has 34-bit instructions and 14-bit addresses. If there are 60 two-address instructions and 65000 one-address instructions, what is the maximum number of zero-address instructions?
questions.solution: A two-address instruction leaves 34−2×14 = 6 opcode bits. The opcode-extension allocation for one-address and zero-address instructions is not sufficiently specified; the provided values/options do not yield a unique standard result.

questions.title: Instruction Count for Four-Bit Opcode
questions.question: If an opcode is 4 bits long, what are the maximum and minimum numbers of instruction types it can support?
questions.solution: A 4-bit opcode can encode 2⁴ = 16 distinct values. Depending on the instruction-set design, all 16 or even zero encodings may be assigned to instructions; the question's 'maximum minimum' phrasing is ambiguous. If asking maximum and minimum nonzero instruction count, option (c) may be intended.

chapters.title: Computer Organization — I/O Organization and Interrupts

questions.title: I/O Module Functions
questions.question: Which of the following is not a major function of an I/O module?
questions.solution: SIMD is a parallel-computing architecture category, not a major I/O-module function.

questions.title: Interrupt versus Programmed I/O Speedup
questions.question: A system has a data transfer rate of 10 KB/s. Calculate the performance gain when an I/O device operates in interrupt mode rather than programmed I/O mode. Interrupt-interface overhead is 15 µs. Round to 1 decimal place.
questions.solution: The amount of data transferred per operation and the processor time spent polling in programmed I/O are not specified, so the speedup cannot be uniquely calculated from the provided data.

questions.title: Programmed I/O Transfer Time
questions.question: In programmed I/O execution, transfer time depends on:
options: Latency of the I/O interface chip
questions.solution: Transfer time can depend on device speed, amount of data transferred, and interface latency.

questions.title: Programmed I/O versus Interrupt Mode
questions.question: Calculate the speedup when an I/O device operates under programmed I/O rather than interrupt mode.
questions.solution: No numerical scenario or timing values are included in the supplied question, so a numerical answer cannot be determined.

questions.title: Software-Generated Interrupts
questions.question: Interrupts caused by software instructions are known as:
questions.solution: Software-generated interrupts are commonly treated as software interrupts/traps or exceptions, depending on the architecture. Of the listed choices, exception interrupt is the closest match.

questions.title: DMA Transfer Cycles
questions.question: A 16-MB/s I/O device is interfaced to a 32-bit CPU using DMA. DMA has a 16-bit count register, a 32-bit data register, and five 8-bit address registers. A data file is 512 KB. How many DMA cycles are required to transfer the file?
questions.solution: If one DMA cycle transfers the 32-bit data-register width (4 bytes), then 512 KB / 4 bytes = 131072 cycles. The listed address-register details and transfer rate do not change this count under that assumption.

questions.title: Word-Addressable Memory Address Bus
questions.question: A processor supports a maximum memory of 32 GB, with word-addressable memory and 1 word = 2 bytes. What is the minimum address-bus size in bits?
questions.solution: 32 GB = 2³⁵ bytes. With 2 bytes per addressable word, the number of addressable words is 2³⁴, requiring 34 address bits.
